1.pericope_label: Remember now thy Creator in the days of thy youth, while the evil days come not... While the sun, or the light, or the moon, or the stars, be not darkened, nor the clouds return after the rain

schools.summary: Delitzsch takes the days of evil for feeble and helpless age and rejects the reading that turns the darkening sky into a storm gathering before death; Ellicott notes that the divine name here stands in the plural like Elohim, and then declines to compete with the imagery at all, owning frankly that after using all the help his predecessors gave him he can offer no more than a vague account of the figures in the passage.

Gill takes the plural at face value and finds three persons in it, assigning creation to Father, Son and Spirit in turn, and prefers to read the darkened lights of the faculties of the soul rather than of failing eyesight, since dim sight is described later in its own right.

Clarke destroys the argument from the plural on manuscript evidence, turns the verse into a claim of divine ownership over the young, and reads the first half of the second verse of the prime of life with the returning clouds as the winter of age; Wesley presses the timing of the duty three ways and offers the face or the outward circumstances as what the darkening describes.

Henry reads the command twice over, as the preacher's application of all he has said about vanity and as the physician's antidote to the diseases of youth, and takes the days of youth for the days of choice, in which a man begins as he means to continue.

debates.question: Does the plural of Creator support the doctrine of the Trinity?

positions.view: Yes; more than one was concerned in creation, and neither more nor fewer than three — Father, Son and Spirit.
The plural stands, on the analogy of the divine name and of other places where Maker is plural.

No; the word is singular in a hundred and seventy-six of Kennicott's manuscripts and ninety-six of De Rossi's, in many old editions and in all the ancient versions, so the support is precarious and ought not to be pressed.

debates.question: What is darkened when the lights fail?

positions.view: The faculties of the soul — understanding, judgment and will — rather than the eyes, whose failure is described separately later.
The face, whose complexion and lively eyes fade, or else the outward circumstances in which youth's joy turns to sorrow.
Nothing yet: the first half describes the prime of life, and only the returning clouds bring on the winter of age.
The onset of feeble old age, described allegorically; not a storm gathering before death.

outliers.note: Turns a textual note into a general warning that men who load doubtful texts with doctrinal weight do the truth no service, and whatever their intentions are its worst friends, their help being assistance to its adversaries.

Declines the whole allegory in advance, observing that readers gain very little from commentators' attempts to explain the silver cord and the golden bowl, and confessing that he himself can give no more than a vague account of the imagery.

themes: Remember now thy Creator in the days of thy youth, while the evil days come not, nor the years draw nigh, when thou shalt say, I have no pleasure in them;
While the sun, or the light, or the moon, or the stars, be not darkened, nor the clouds return after the rain:

3.pericope_label: In the day when the keepers of the house shall tremble, and the strong men shall bow themselves... Then shall the dust return to the earth as it was: and the spirit shall return unto God who gave it

schools.summary: Delitzsch reports without embarrassment the old Jewish reading of the doors as the body's apertures, citing the morning benediction that blesses God for forming man with cavities, and describes the passage's architecture as three successive clauses moving from general discomfort through the forerunners of death to the dissolution itself; Ellicott begins from the household rather than the body and warns that finding an anatomical equivalent for every image makes the reading forced.

Gill canvasses the older identifications of the keepers — knees, ribs, hands — before following Aben Ezra to the hands and arms, prefers the lips for the doors of the fourth verse, and mentions a reading that made the silver cord the string of the tongue.

Clarke numbers the members as he goes, hands, legs, teeth and optic nerves, and identifies the silver cord as the spinal marrow and the golden bowl as the brain, adding that the falling of the lower jaw is the one infallible sign of death; Wesley gives the same identifications more briefly and takes the man to rise as the birds begin.

debates.question: How far should the allegory be carried?

positions.view: All the way; every member has its figure, from the palsied hands to the thickening humours of the eye.
The house means the body, but pressing an anatomical equivalent for every image makes the reading so forced that some prefer to read the verse as general alarm at a storm.
Partly; the older identifications are canvassed and chosen among rather than multiplied.
The structure matters more than the parts: three clauses moving from discomfort through the forerunners of death to dissolution.
It blossoms white, an emblem of a hoary head — though the verb means to fall off rather than to flourish, the hair whitening and dropping for want of nourishment.
It causes loathing; the locust, elsewhere a favourite food, becomes a burden, and the caper berry fails.
It flowers, and the head is as full of grey hairs as the tree is of white flowers.

outliers.note: Sets out three interpretations of the voice of the bird, says each meets serious objections, and declines to argue any of them, having nothing better to propose himself.

Refuses to draw consolation from the returning spirit, holding that the notion of a personal spirit going to God with its consciousness intact is foreign to the verse, while allowing that what the book earlier left an open question is here stated as fact.

themes: In the day when the keepers of the house shall tremble, and the strong men shall bow themselves, and the grinders cease because they are few, and those that look out of the windows be darkened,
And the doors shall be shut in the streets, when the sound of the grinding is low, and he shall rise up at the voice of the bird, and all the daughters of musick shall be brought low;

Also when they shall be afraid of that which is high, and fears shall be in the way, and the almond tree shall flourish, and the grasshopper shall be a burden, and desire shall fail: because man goeth to his long home, and the mourners go about the streets:
Or ever the silver cord be loosed, or the golden bowl be broken, or the pitcher be broken at the fountain, or the wheel broken at the cistern.
Then shall the dust return to the earth as it was: and the spirit shall return unto God who gave it.

8.pericope_label: Vanity of vanities, saith the preacher; all is vanity... of making many books there is no end; and much study is a weariness of the flesh

schools.summary: Delitzsch insists that the conjunction opening the postscript is only an external join and that nothing is more unwarranted than making the motto its first sentence, rejects a rendering by which it remains to be added that Koheleth was wise, and establishes the goad from the Greek versions and a rabbinic list of driving-rods; Ellicott holds the epilogue an integral part of the book whose author now speaks in his own person, and confesses that the words of the eleventh verse are enigmatical and their precise sense uncertain.

Gill treats the repeated motto as a proposition now proved by an induction of particulars, insists that acceptable words means doctrines rather than an elegant style, and takes the goad as it stands, a sharp stick applied to doctrine that pierces the heart.

Clarke lets the picture of dissolution enforce the motto, reports and then doubts an elaborate theory that the masters of assemblies were licensers appointed to keep unprofitable matter from the people, and answers the warning against many books by observing that millions of treatises have since been added and no subject is exhausted; Wesley makes the masters the teachers of the church and the one shepherd Christ.

Henry has the preacher unwilling to part with his hearers until he carries his point, and builds up his credentials as a penitent gathered home from his wanderings, a man wiser than his neighbours, and one who used his wisdom to do good.

positions.view: A second writer, speaking in his own name after recording the preacher's words, who tells his readers that the man he has been quoting was also an author.
The author who had introduced Koheleth as the speaker, now continuing on his own account.
The preacher himself, recommending his own writings and those of other wise men.

debates.question: What are the masters of assemblies?

positions.view: Teachers of the church, appointed by God, whose words come from the one Shepherd.
Possibly officers appointed to license what reached the people, though such officials are little more than conjecture, and the phrase may simply mean public teachers.
Uncertain; the term might as easily mean collections of sayings as gatherings of people, and nothing can be made of the closing clause beyond the sages being given to instruct the people.
The inspired penmen of scripture and all good men whose doctrine agrees with them.

outliers.note: Answers the warning against many books from two thousand years' distance, observing that millions of treatises have since been added, that the press is still groaning, and that we know nothing certainly from any of them except what bears the seal of God.
Frames the two verses as a contrast between the weighty sayings of ancient sages and the volubility of modern bookmakers.

themes: Vanity of vanities, saith the preacher; all is vanity.
And moreover, because the preacher was wise, he still taught the people knowledge; yea, he gave good heed, and sought out, and set in order many proverbs.
The preacher sought to find out acceptable words: and that which was written was upright, even words of truth.
The words of the wise are as goads, and as nails fastened by the masters of assemblies, which are given from one shepherd.
And further, by these, my son, be admonished: of making many books there is no end; and much study is a weariness of the flesh.

13.pericope_label: Let us hear the conclusion of the whole matter: Fear God, and keep his commandments... For God shall bring every work into judgment, with every secret thing, whether it be good, or whether it be evil

schools.summary: Delitzsch treats the opening phrase as a heading giving the final result once all is learned, and rejects the rendering that turns it into an invitation for us all to listen, since the pronoun would then be used of persons where this author uses it of things; he reads the closing clause as an obligation lying on every man without exception, and presses the concealment of the last verse, a judgment from which nothing hidden escapes. Ellicott renders the duty of every man rather than the whole duty of man, and argues that the announced judgment can only be one after death.
Gill hears a closing formula in which everything worth regard is compressed into a few words, and refers the judgment, with the Targum, to the great day rather than to this life.

Clarke objects that the noun duty was supplied by the translators and spoils the sense, the Hebrew saying the whole of Adam; he reduces the commandments to the two on which they hang, sets out the reasons for the judgment in numbered steps, and closes the book on the observation that although here all is vanity, there vanities will be vain no more; Wesley takes the fear of God for the whole inward worship of God and extends the last clause to secret thoughts.

Henry states the question the book has pursued and finds the answer here, that serious godliness is the only way to happiness, locates the root of religion in a fear reigning in the heart, and makes a point of the preacher saying Let us hear rather than Do you hear.

debates.question: What does the closing clause of the thirteenth verse say?

positions.view: The whole of Adam; the word duty was supplied by the translators and spoils, perhaps perverts, the sense.
The duty of every man rather than the whole duty of man, anticipating the apostle's argument that God is not the God of one nation only.
An obligation lying on every man without exception.
A man's whole work, his whole perfection, and the sum of all he needs to know or do or enjoy.

outliers.note: Makes the final verse decisive for the whole book: since the work is filled with complaints about the imperfection of earthly retribution, the judgment announced here can only be one after death, so that a book of sceptical debate ends by stating the doctrine of a day when God judges the secrets of men more plainly than anywhere else in the Old Testament.

Notes that the Hebrew scribes marked this verse as weighty by beginning it with an enlarged letter, and presses the preacher's own inclusion in his exhortation: a man who teaches others and not himself is a teacher by halves.

themes: Let us hear the conclusion of the whole matter: Fear God, and keep his commandments: for this is the whole duty of man.
For God shall bring every work into judgment, with every secret thing, whether it be good, or whether it be evil.
